input:
I hold up a hand to the others. "Darkness, you're practically vibrating. Take Aqua and Megumin and go scout those sewers. Luna wants a word, and honestly, one conversation at a time is all I can handle before noon."

I push back from the table and head toward the reception desk, leaving them to sort out who carries the torch.

messages.content:
Aqua's mug freezes halfway to her lips. Her eyes go wide and wet with the first shimmer of tears. The sewers. You are sending her to the *sewers*. Before noon. Without you.

Darkness, by contrast, looks like you just handed her a birthday present wrapped in mortal peril. Her gauntlets clench the table's edge, and a flush creeps up her neck at the thought of Brutal Alligators lurking in those dark, filthy tunnels — creatures famous for grappling their prey and dragging it under.

Megumin opens one eye. The other remains hidden beneath her eyepatch as she slumps against the table, her legs still useless from this morning's dawn Explosion. She cannot walk to the sewers. She cannot walk to the door. She could, at best, be rolled.

You push back from the table before any of them can muster a full objection, and make your way across the guild hall toward the reception desk.

Behind you, a chair scrapes. Darkness is already standing, breathless with barely contained enthusiasm. Aqua is wailing something about divine dignity and filth. Megumin, with the weary patience of the party's sole voice of reason, appears to be negotiating the logistics of being carried.

Luna watches your approach from behind the desk. Her professional smile is fixed in place, but her eyes track you the way a clerk tracks a lit fuse rolling toward a powder keg. She already knows how this conversation ends — she has known since she saw your party's tab this morning — and she is already sorry.
The SEWERS?! I am a goddess! A GODDESS, Kazuma! You cannot simply dispatch me into raw sewage like some sort of — of plumbing implement! (slams her mug down, sloshing ale across the table)
messages.speaker: Aqua

messages.content: The sewers. Where Brutal Alligators lurk in the dark, waiting to ambush unwary adventurers... to coil around them and drag them beneath the murky water, helpless and— I mean, yes. A Crusader must scout ahead. It is my duty. (already on her feet, gauntlets trembling slightly)
messages.speaker: Darkness

messages.content: An excellent plan. Truly. Send the archwizard who cannot feel her own legs into a labyrinth of filth. I shall contribute by being carried like a sack of potatoes and offering tactical criticism from approximately knee height. (still slumped dramatically against the table, one hand raised as if delivering a grand proclamation)
messages.speaker: Megumin

messages.content: Good morning. Your party's debt now exceeds the annual budget of several small villages. I have a quest. I am... sorry. (folds her hands on the counter, smile tightening at the corners)
messages.speaker: Luna

input: I reach the desk and plant both palms on the worn wood. "Alright, Luna. You've got that look — the one that says 'I'm about to ruin someone's day and I've already decided it's yours.' Let's hear it."

messages.content:
Luna's professional smile doesn't waver, but something behind her eyes tightens — the expression of a woman who has learned, through long and bitter experience, exactly how much paperwork one adventuring party can generate. She glances past you at the now-empty table where Aqua left a small lake of spilled ale, then back to you with the resigned weariness of someone who has already started filling out the incident report in her head.

She reaches below the counter and produces a ledger thick enough to stop a sword. The cover is worn soft from handling. She opens it to a page marked with a crimson ribbon, turns it to face you, and taps a single figure at the bottom with a manicured nail. The number is long enough that it takes you a moment to count the digits.

input: I lean over the ledger, find the number at the bottom, and stare at it for a long, hollow moment. "That's... that's not a debt. That's a national deficit with my name on it."

messages.content:
Luna doesn't flinch. She's done the math already — probably did it three times, late last night, hoping the numbers would somehow come out different. They never do.

She turns the ledger back toward herself with the practiced efficiency of someone who has learned not to dwell on the horror. One finger traces down the column of fines, stopping at a line item that just says *"Explosion (unpermitted, downtown) — See Attached (pages 4–17)."* Her professional smile holds steady, but there's a flicker behind it — something almost sympathetic, buried under layers of bureaucratic exhaustion.

Then she reaches beneath the counter and produces a single quest parchment. The paper is yellowed. The ink is faded. This thing has been sitting on the board for a very, very long time.

I am so very sorry. That is not a joke. However, I do have a quest that would... substantially reduce this balance. No one else will take it. No one else ever has. (slides the yellowed parchment across the counter toward you)
messages.speaker: Luna

input: I drag my eyes away from the debt figure and pick up the yellowed parchment. "Alright. What's the catch? If no one's taken this in... how many years exactly?"

messages.content:
Luna's eyes flick to the parchment in your hands, then away — toward the window, toward the morning light, toward anywhere that isn't the yellowed relic you're now holding. For the first time all morning, her professional smile falters. Not into guilt, exactly. Something closer to embarrassment.

She busies her hands with the ledger, closing it, stacking it, aligning its corners with the edge of the desk. When she finally looks back at you, there's something almost human behind the receptionist mask. The expression of a woman who has handed this same parchment to seventeen different adventurers across seventeen different years, and watched every single one of them slide it back across the counter with the same look of dawning horror.

The paper crackles as your thumb brushes the date stamp in the corner. The ink is so faded it's nearly ghosted into the fibers. You have to squint to even make out the year.

She doesn't sugarcoat it. Luna has never sugarcoated anything in her life — sugarcoating requires optimism, and optimism requires not knowing exactly how poorly things can go. She folds her hands on the desk, her posture straight and proper, and delivers the facts the way a surgeon delivers a prognosis.

Forty-seven years. The catch is... well, the catch is why it's been forty-seven years. It's a purification request for an old shrine in the mountains east of town. The last party that tried came back two weeks later with half their members and wouldn't speak of what they saw. The five parties before that didn't come back at all. (Her voice stays level, but her knuckles are white where her hands clasp together.)
messages.speaker: Luna

messages.content: The pay would clear your debt entirely. That's why I'm showing it to you. I'm not... I wouldn't normally. But you're the only party in Axel reckless enough to maybe survive it, and I thought you deserved to at least know the option exists. (She meets your eyes and holds them. The sympathy is real, even if it's buried under three layers of bureaucratic exhaustion.)
messages.speaker: Luna

input:
I stare at the faded date stamp a moment longer, then let out a slow breath. "Forty-seven years. Seventeen attempts. And you're offering this to the guy whose party includes a goddess who cries over spilled ale, a pervert crusader, and a wizard who collapses after one spell."

I don't put the parchment down.

"What exactly is *at* that shrine?"

messages.content:
Luna doesn't answer right away. Instead she reaches across the counter and gently — almost reverently — takes the parchment back from your hands. She doesn't look at it. She's probably memorized every word by now.

She sets it down between you, smoothing its curled edges with the heel of her palm. The gesture is careful, precise, the same way she aligns the corners of her ledger. But her hand lingers on the parchment a moment too long.

When she finally meets your eyes, the professional smile is gone. What's left is something rawer — the expression of a woman who has been carrying a secret she never wanted to keep, and is too tired to keep pretending it doesn't weigh on her.

She draws a slow breath through her nose, and you realize she's not stalling anymore. She's steeling herself.

input: I don't look away. I don't put the parchment down either.

messages.content:
Luna meets your eyes — really meets them, not the professional once-over she gives every adventurer who darkens her counter. There are faint lines at the corners of her eyes that you've never noticed before. Lines that didn't come from squinting at ledgers.

Her palm flattens against the parchment. The hand is trembling, just barely. She's not trying to hide it anymore.

She draws a breath that catches somewhere in her throat, and for a moment she looks less like a guild receptionist and more like someone standing at the edge of something she's been walking away from for nearly half her life.

I was seventeen. My party — four of us, all C-rank, all convinced we were invincible — took this quest because no one else would. We thought that was the same thing as being ready. (Her voice is quieter than you've ever heard it, stripped of every scrap of professional polish.)
messages.speaker: Luna

messages.content: Only two of us came back down that mountain. And I've spent every year since — forty-seven of them — sitting behind this counter, watching other adventurers, wondering if I should have died up there too. (She doesn't look away. Her jaw is set, but her eyes are wet.)
messages.speaker: Luna
